units.t: Mental Maths Shortcuts.
Part one. Tens, fives and fifteens.
Here's a secret that people who are good at mental maths rarely admit.
They aren't doing harder sums than you.
They're doing easier ones.
They break an awkward number into friendly pieces, work out each piece, and add them back together.
That's the whole game, and by the end of this lesson you'll have a handful of those friendly pieces ready to use.
If you're driving, don't try to work anything out.
Just listen along, and try the tricks later when you're standing at a counter.
Let's start with percentages, because they're everywhere.
The friendliest percentage of all is ten per cent.
To find ten per cent of anything, you just move the decimal point one place to the left.
Ten per cent of $86 is $8.60.
Ten per cent of $240 is $24.
Ten per cent of $7.50 is seventy-five cents.
Once you have ten per cent, a whole family of other percentages falls out of it.
Five per cent is half of ten per cent.
So five per cent of $86 is half of $8.60, which is $4.30.
Twenty per cent is double ten per cent, so that's $17.20.
And fifteen per cent is just ten per cent plus five per cent.
Add $8.60 and $4.30 and you get $12.90.
Tipping isn't expected in Australia the way it is in the United States, because hospitality wages here don't depend on tips.
But plenty of people like to leave something for great service, or chip in extra at a group dinner.
With ten per cent in your pocket, a tip becomes a two-second job.
For a rough ten per cent, move the decimal and round up to a tidy number.
Now here's a trick that genuinely surprises people.
Percentages can be flipped.
Eight per cent of fifty is exactly the same as fifty per cent of eight.
And fifty per cent of eight is easy.
It's four.
So eight per cent of fifty is four.
This works every time, because a percentage is really just two numbers multiplied together and divided by one hundred.
The order doesn't matter.
So when a percentage looks nasty, swap it around and see if it gets nicer.
Four per cent of seventy-five sounds awkward.
Seventy-five per cent of four is three.
Twelve per cent of twenty-five becomes twenty-five per cent of twelve, which is a quarter of twelve.
That's three again.
One more Australian special.
Most prices you see here already include the goods and services tax, which is ten per cent.
You might think the tax inside a price is a tenth of it, but it isn't.
It's one eleventh.
That's because the price is the original amount plus another ten per cent on top, so it's eleven parts, and the tax is one of them.
On a $110 bill, the tax is $10, not $11.
On a $55 item, it's $5.
When a price divides neatly by eleven, you can find the tax almost instantly.
In the next part, we'll take these ideas to the restaurant table and look at splitting a bill without reaching for your phone.
Part two. Splitting the bill.
Dividing in your head feels harder than multiplying, mostly because we try to do it in one big step.
The trick is to break it into small steps that you already know.
Splitting between two people is just halving, and most of us are comfortable with that.
Splitting between four is halving twice.
Say the bill is $236 and there are four of you.
Half of $236 is $118.
Half of $118 is $59.
That's $59 each, and you never had to divide by four.
Splitting between eight is halving three times.
Splitting between six is halving, then dividing by three.
For a $150 bill between six, half is $75, and a third of $75 is $25.
Dividing by five has a lovely shortcut too.
Double the number, then divide by ten.
A $130 bill between five people becomes $260, and then $26 each.
It works because dividing by five is the same as dividing by ten and multiplying by two, and the order of those doesn't matter either.
When a bill doesn't split evenly, round first and tidy up after.
Say it's $97 between three.
Ninety-nine would split nicely into three lots of $33.
So think of it as $33 each, less a couple of dollars off the total.
In practice, two people pay $32 and one pays $33, or everyone pays $33 and the extra two dollars becomes the tip.
Near enough really is good enough at dinner.
The same round-and-adjust idea is brilliant for multiplying prices that end in ninety-five or ninety-nine cents.
Four items at $19.95 each looks fiddly.
But each one is five cents short of $20.
Four lots of $20 is $80, and four lots of five cents is twenty cents.
So the total is $80 less twenty cents, which is $79.80.
Round-and-adjust works when adding a list, too.
At the supermarket, round each item to the nearest dollar as it goes into the trolley.
Some of your roundings go up and some go down, so the errors tend to cancel out.
By the checkout you'll usually be within a few dollars of the real total, which is plenty accurate for a sense of where you stand.
Now for the most useful skill of all, especially around the big sales.
Working out what a discount is really worth.
Part three. Discounts and deals.
When you see thirty per cent off, there are two ways to think about it.
You can work out the discount and subtract it.
Or you can go straight to what you'll pay.
Thirty per cent off means you pay seventy per cent.
For an $80 jacket, ten per cent is $8, so seventy per cent is seven lots of $8.
That's $56.
One step instead of two.
Here's where many shoppers get caught.
Stacked discounts don't simply add up.
Imagine a store offering twenty per cent off, with an extra ten per cent off at the register.
It sounds like thirty per cent off.
It isn't.
The extra ten per cent comes off the already reduced price, not the original one.
Take a $100 item.
Twenty per cent off brings it to $80.
Then ten per cent off $80 is $8, which brings it to $72.
So the real discount is twenty-eight per cent, not thirty.
On a small purchase that barely matters.
On a fridge or a couch, it's real money, and it's worth knowing before a sign convinces you otherwise.
The same thinking helps with the classic multi-buy offers.
Buy two, get one free sounds generous, and it is.
You get three items for the price of two, which works out to a third off each one.
Compare that with second item half price.
There you pay for one and a half items and get two, which is a quarter off each.
So buy two get one free is the better deal, but only if you'd genuinely use all three.
And percentages have one last trap that catches almost everyone.
Going up and coming back down by the same percentage doesn't bring you back to where you started.
If a share price rises fifty per cent and then falls fifty per cent, you don't break even.
A hundred dollars becomes one hundred and fifty, and then half of that is seventy-five.
The fall is taken from a bigger number, so it bites harder.
Finally, when you're comparing packet sizes, lean on the unit price.
Large Australian supermarkets are required to show a unit price on the shelf label, such as the price per hundred grams or per litre.
Bigger packs are often cheaper per unit, but not always, and specials can flip the usual pattern.
That small number on the label does the mental maths for you, so glance at it before you reach for the bigger box.
So here's what to carry with you.
Build every percentage from ten per cent, flip a percentage when it looks awkward, and remember that the tax inside a price is one eleventh.
Split bills by halving and by rounding then adjusting.
And with discounts, think about what you'll actually pay, because stacked deals are always a little less generous than they sound.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. What's the quickest way to find fifteen per cent of a bill?
Answer. Find ten per cent, halve it to get five per cent, then add the two together.
Question two. If a price includes GST, what fraction of the price is the tax?
Answer. One eleventh.
Question three. Twenty per cent off, then an extra ten per cent off. What's the real total discount?
Answer. Twenty-eight per cent, not thirty.
That's the end of Mental Maths Shortcuts. Nice work. Enjoy that next bill.
